Cut Cube

GeometryCoordinatesTriangles
What it shows: A cube and a flat sheet, with the outline showing where the sheet passes through the cube.
How to play: Drag a dot to slide or tilt the sheet, or drag the picture to turn the cube. Press a shape button to see a triangular, square, four-, five- or six-sided cut.

Drag with the left button to turn, with the right button to slide, and with Alt held down to zoom. On a keyboard: arrows turn, + and − zoom, and comma and full stop move the sheet.

Look for the math

One straight sheet can pass through a cube in surprisingly many ways. The coloured outline is the cross section: the shape the sheet and the solid have in common.

One side for each face

Write the sheet as ax + by + cz = d. A corner of the outline can only appear where the sheet crosses an edge of the cube, and an edge belongs to two faces. The outline therefore has one side for each cube face the sheet meets. A polyhedron with six faces can give at most six sides. The logic test checked every integer direction with coordinates from −3 to 3 and many heights: no cut had seven sides, though three, four, five and six all occurred.

The shapes the page asks for

The page asks whether the section can be a square, a quadrilateral, a pentagon or a hexagon. All four are possible, and the five buttons above show them. A sheet parallel to a face, z = 0, gives a square. A tilted sheet such as x + y = 1 gives a quadrilateral that is not a square. x + y + 0.8z = 1.6 gives five sides, and x + y + z = 0 through the centre gives a regular hexagon. Every outline point really satisfies the sheet's equation and lies on the cube.

Moving and showing

Turning or sliding the cube changes the numbers a, b, c, d, but the shape of the cut stays the same as long as the two objects keep the same relative position. That is why the "combined" choice carries the cube along when the sheet moves: it is the same cut viewed from another place. "Transparent" and "opaque" only change how the sheet is drawn; neither changes the cut.

Cutting off a pyramid

Choose x + y + z = 7.5 and the sheet passes just beyond the corner (3, 3, 3). It meets the three edges at that corner, leaving a triangle behind and cutting off a small tetrahedron — a pyramid with a triangular base. The test confirmed that exactly one corner is on the far side of the sheet.

Try the six-sided cut, then slide the sheet slowly towards a corner and watch the outline shrink from six sides to five, four and three.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
